column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is the name of the shape of a DNA molecule?
column28: DNA is a double helix: two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. A common mistake is saying single helix, but DNA has two strands, not one.
column29: Think about how many strands DNA has and what twisted shape they make.

column9: DNA is a long polymer. What is the name of the small repeating unit (monomer) that DNA is built from?
column28: DNA is a nucleic acid, and the monomer of a nucleic acid is the nucleotide. Amino acids build proteins, monosaccharides build carbohydrates, and fatty acids are part of lipids; mixing up the monomers of the four biomolecules is the common mistake.
column29: The monomer's name sounds like the word nucleic.

column9: The five-carbon sugar found in every DNA nucleotide is called ___.
column28: The sugar in DNA is deoxyribose; that is where the D in DNA comes from. Ribose is the sugar in RNA, and glucose is not part of DNA at all.
column29: The name of the sugar is hidden in the full name of DNA: ___nucleic acid.

column9: Which of these is NOT found in a DNA molecule?
column28: Uracil (U) is found in RNA, not DNA. DNA uses thymine (T) instead, and it also contains the sugar deoxyribose and phosphate groups. Putting U into DNA is a very common mistake.
column29: One of these is the base RNA uses in place of thymine.

column9: In a DNA double helix, adenine (A) always pairs with which base?
column28: The base pairing rule says A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Uracil pairs with A only in RNA, and pairing A with G is the common mix-up.
column29: Remember the pairs as two teams: A with one letter, C with the other.

column9: In a DNA sequence such as ATGC, what does the letter G stand for?
column28: G stands for guanine, one of the four nitrogen bases (A, T, C, G). Glucose is a sugar and glycine is an amino acid; neither one is a DNA base.
column29: Each letter in a DNA sequence is the first letter of a nitrogen base.

column9: Which type of bond holds the two bases of a base pair together in the middle of the DNA molecule?
column28: Weak hydrogen bonds hold the paired bases together across the middle of the helix. Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, which students sometimes confuse with DNA.
column29: These bonds are weak enough that the two strands can be pulled apart.

column9: What does the abbreviation DNA stand for?
column28: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid: deoxyribo- for its sugar (deoxyribose) and nucleic acid for its biomolecule group. It is not an amino acid; amino acids build proteins.
column29: The first part of the name is the name of DNA's sugar.

column9: How many strands make up one DNA double helix?
column28: A double helix has two strands that twist around each other. RNA is usually a single strand, which is why some students answer one.
column29: The word double is a clue.

column9: Why is the shape of DNA described as a double helix?
column14: Because DNA is twice as long as RNA
column15: Because DNA has two kinds of sugar
column16: Because DNA copies itself twice before a cell divides
column17: Because DNA has two strands twisted around each other
column28: Double means two strands, and helix means a spiral twist. DNA has only one kind of sugar (deoxyribose), and its length has nothing to do with the name.
column29: Break the name into two words and ask what each word describes.

column9: Which two scientists are credited with building the first accurate model of the DNA double helix in 1953?
column16: Robert Hooke and Anton van Leeuwenhoek
column28: Watson and Crick built the double helix model in 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and base data from Erwin Chargaff. Mendel studied inheritance in peas, and Hooke and Leeuwenhoek worked on cells and microscopes.
column29: Their names are often said together, like a team.

column9: What was Rosalind Franklin's key contribution to figuring out the structure of DNA?
column14: She discovered that traits are passed down in predictable patterns
column15: She found that the amount of A equals the amount of T
column16: She took X-ray images of DNA, including the famous Photo 51
column17: She built a metal model of DNA and won the Nobel Prize for it
column28: Franklin used X-ray crystallography to make images of DNA, including Photo 51. Chargaff found that A = T, Mendel studied inheritance patterns, and Watson and Crick built the model. A common mistake is giving Franklin credit for the model or giving Watson and Crick credit for the X-ray image.
column29: Her work used a special kind of imaging that bounces X-rays off a molecule.

column9: You scrape a few cells from the inside of your cheek. Where is most of the DNA in each of those cells found?
column28: In human (eukaryotic) cells, most DNA is in the nucleus, packed into chromosomes. Animal cells have no cell wall, and the membrane and vacuole do not store DNA.
column29: Which organelle is called the control center of the cell?

column9: In a DNA molecule, the two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases.
column28: True. The bases pair in the middle of the helix (A with T, C with G), and weak hydrogen bonds hold each pair together. A common mistake is thinking the sugars or phosphates connect the two strands.
column29: Picture the rungs of a ladder: what holds the two halves of each rung together?

column9: A student builds a DNA model out of candy. Licorice sticks make the two long sides, and gumdrops stuck on toothpicks make the bases. What should the licorice sides represent?
column28: The sides of DNA are the sugar-phosphate backbone: deoxyribose, phosphate, deoxyribose, phosphate. The bases are already the gumdrops, and they form the rungs. Putting the bases on the sides is the common mistake.
column29: The gumdrops are already the bases. What else is in a nucleotide?

column9: You are building one DNA nucleotide from a model kit. Select every piece you need. Select all that apply.
column28: A DNA nucleotide has a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and one nitrogen base. Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides, amino acids build proteins, and fatty acids build lipids.
column29: A nucleotide has three parts. One is a sugar; make sure it is the DNA sugar.

column9: Select every nitrogen base that is found in DNA. Select all that apply.
column28: DNA has four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, and glucose is a sugar, not a base.
column29: DNA has four bases. Remember the letters A, T, C and G.

column9: Match each DNA base to the base it pairs with on the opposite strand.
column28: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, in either direction. The common mistake is pairing A with G or C with T.
column29: A and T go together; C and G go together.

column9: DNA is often compared to a twisted ladder. Match each part of the ladder to the part of DNA it represents.
column14: The two side rails :: Alternating sugar and phosphate (the backbone)
column15: The rungs :: Pairs of nitrogen bases
column16: Where the two halves of a rung meet :: Weak hydrogen bonds
column17: Twisting the whole ladder into a spiral :: The double helix shape
column28: The sides are the sugar-phosphate backbone, each rung is a base pair, hydrogen bonds hold the two bases of a rung together, and the twist makes the double helix. Swapping the sides and the rungs is the most common mistake.
column29: Start with the rungs: they connect the two strands, so they must be the parts that pair up.

column9: Match each DNA term to its meaning.
column14: Nucleotide :: A phosphate, a sugar and a nitrogen base joined together
column15: Deoxyribose :: The five-carbon sugar in DNA
column16: Base pair :: Two bases joined across the middle of the helix, such as A and T
column17: Double helix :: Two strands twisted around each other
column18: Nitrogen base :: The part of a nucleotide that acts as a letter of the genetic code
column28: A nucleotide is the full building block, deoxyribose is its sugar, a base pair is two bases joined across the helix, the double helix is the twisted two-strand shape, and the nitrogen base is the letter (A, T, C or G). Mixing up nucleotide (the whole unit) with nitrogen base (one part) is common.
column29: Match the biggest unit (nucleotide) first, then its parts.

column9: One DNA strand reads TACG. The complementary (matching) strand reads ___.
column20: ATGC|A T G C|A-T-G-C|A, T, G, C|A,T,G,C
column28: T pairs with A, A with T, C with G and G with C, so TACG pairs with ATGC. Writing U instead of T is a common mistake because U is only in RNA.
column29: Go one letter at a time: write each base's partner.

column9: A short stretch of yeast DNA reads CCATGA on one strand. The complementary strand reads ___.
column20: GGTACT|G G T A C T|G-G-T-A-C-T|G, G, T, A, C, T|G,G,T,A,C,T
column28: C→G, C→G, A→T, T→A, G→C, A→T gives GGTACT. A common mistake is writing the same sequence backward instead of pairing each base.
column29: Pair each base in order from left to right: C goes with G, and A goes with T.

column9: One strand of DNA reads A-G-C-T. Which sequence is on the complementary strand?
column28: A→T, G→C, C→G, T→A gives T-C-G-A. U-C-G-A would be an RNA partner, and A-G-C-T just copies the strand instead of pairing it.
column29: Find the partner of each letter, keeping the same order.

column9: All DNA nucleotides share some parts, but one part can be different from one nucleotide to the next. Which part changes and gives DNA its letters?
column28: Every DNA nucleotide has the same phosphate and the same sugar; only the nitrogen base (A, T, C or G) changes. That is why we write DNA as a string of base letters.
column29: DNA is written with four letters. What do those letters name?

column9: The bases A, T, C and G are called the letters of DNA. What do these letters spell out?
column14: Instructions for building proteins and traits
column15: The amount of energy the cell has stored
column16: The type of sugar the cell will eat
column17: The thickness of the cell membrane
column28: The order of the bases carries genetic information: instructions for making proteins, which shape an organism's traits. DNA does not store energy; that is the job of molecules like ATP and glucose.
column29: Why do children look like their parents?

column9: Inside one DNA nucleotide, which part is the nitrogen base attached directly to?
column16: The base on the other strand
column17: Another phosphate on the same strand
column28: In a nucleotide the base is attached to the sugar, and the phosphate is attached to the other side of the sugar. The base also pairs with a base on the other strand, but that is a weak hydrogen bond between nucleotides, not a part of one nucleotide.
column29: The sugar sits in the middle of the nucleotide, between the other two parts.

column9: DNA belongs to which group of biomolecules?
column28: DNA is a nucleic acid (the NA in DNA). It contains a sugar, but it is not a carbohydrate, and it carries instructions for proteins but is not a protein itself.
column29: Look at the last two letters of DNA.

column9: The hydrogen bonds between base pairs are weak. Why is that useful for the cell?
column14: The two strands can be pulled apart (unzipped) when DNA is copied or read
column15: DNA can dissolve completely in water
column16: The bases can swap partners whenever they want, so any base can pair with any other base
column17: The backbone can break apart easily
column28: Weak hydrogen bonds let the strands separate like a zipper, so each strand can be copied or read, and then zip back together. The bases do not swap partners randomly, and the backbone is held by strong bonds, not weak ones.
column29: Think of a zipper: it is useful because it opens and closes easily.

column9: Which scientist discovered that in any DNA sample, the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine and the amount of cytosine equals the amount of guanine?
column28: Erwin Chargaff measured the bases in DNA from many organisms and found A = T and C = G, now called Chargaff's rule. Mendel worked on inheritance, Hooke named cells and Darwin studied evolution.
column29: The rule about base amounts is named after this scientist.

column9: Bacteria, oak trees and humans all use the same four kinds of nitrogen bases (A, T, C and G) in their DNA.
column28: True. All living things use the same four DNA bases. What makes organisms different is the order of those bases, not new kinds of bases.
column29: Do different organisms need different letters, or the same letters in a different order?

column9: A short stretch of corn DNA reads GGGG on one strand. What sequence is directly across from it on the other strand?
column28: G always pairs with C, so GGGG sits across from CCCC. Copying the same letters (GGGG) is the mistake, because the strands are partners, not copies.
column29: What is G's partner?

column9: A gumdrop DNA model uses red for adenine, blue for thymine, green for cytosine and yellow for guanine. Which color must always be across from a red gumdrop?
column28: Red is adenine, and adenine pairs with thymine, which is blue. Choosing yellow (guanine) is the common mistake of pairing A with G.
column29: Turn the color back into a base letter first, then find its partner.

column9: Which statement correctly describes the base pairing rule in DNA?
column14: A pairs with G, and C pairs with T
column15: Any base can pair with any other base
column16: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G
column17: A pairs with C, and G pairs with T
column28: The rule is A with T and C with G. Bases do not pair randomly; each base has only one partner in DNA.
column29: Think of the pairs as AT and CG.

column9: How many different kinds of nitrogen bases are found in DNA?
column28: DNA has four kinds of bases: A, T, C and G. The number 20 is the number of amino acids, and 64 is the number of codons; those come up later in protein synthesis.
column29: Count the letters used to write a DNA sequence.

column9: Which part of DNA is found in the middle of the double helix, between the two backbones?
column28: The nitrogen bases point inward and pair in the middle of the helix. The sugars and phosphates are on the outside, forming the backbones.
column29: Which part pairs with a partner on the other strand?

column9: Which word describes two DNA strands whose bases fit together as partners, with A across from T and C across from G?
column28: Complementary means the strands match as partners, like puzzle pieces. They are not identical: one strand is not a copy of the other.
column29: This word means two things complete each other.

column9: Photo 51, an X-ray image of DNA, showed an X-shaped pattern. What did that X pattern tell scientists?
column14: That DNA is shaped like a helix (spiral)
column15: That DNA is made of protein
column16: That DNA is found only in the nucleus
column17: That DNA has exactly four bases
column28: The X pattern in Photo 51 is the signature of a helix, which helped Watson and Crick build the double helix model. The image could not show what DNA is made of or where it is in the cell.
column29: Photo 51 was about DNA's shape, not its location or ingredients.

column9: One strand of a DNA segment has 8 bases. How many bases are in the whole double-stranded segment?
column28: Each base on one strand has a partner on the other strand, so 8 bases pair with 8 more: 16 bases in all. Answering 8 forgets the second strand.
column29: Every base has a partner on the other strand.

column9: Which molecule carries the hereditary information that is passed from parents to their offspring?
column28: DNA carries hereditary information in the order of its bases. ATP and glucose are energy molecules, and cholesterol is a lipid.
column29: This molecule is found in chromosomes.

column9: In the twisted-ladder model of DNA, the nitrogen bases form the two sides of the ladder.
column28: False. The sides of the ladder are alternating sugar and phosphate groups. The nitrogen bases form the rungs in the middle. Swapping these two is one of the most common DNA mistakes.
column29: Which part of a nucleotide pairs with a partner across the middle?

column9: A bacterium has no nucleus. Which statement about its DNA is true?
column14: It has no DNA at all
column15: Its DNA is found in the cytoplasm
column16: Its DNA is part of the cell wall
column17: Its DNA is made of protein
column28: Bacteria (prokaryotes) still have DNA, with the same double helix structure; it sits in the cytoplasm instead of a nucleus. Every living cell has DNA.
column29: Every living cell needs instructions. Where could they be if there is no nucleus?

column9: A chromosome is one very long molecule wrapped around proteins and packed tightly. Which molecule is it?
column28: A chromosome is a long DNA double helix wrapped around proteins and packed tightly. Starch and lipids are other biomolecules that do not carry genes.
column29: Genes are found on chromosomes. What are genes made of?

column9: A single DNA strand is 9 nucleotides long. How many deoxyribose sugars does it contain?
column28: Every nucleotide has exactly one deoxyribose sugar, so 9 nucleotides have 9 sugars. Doubling to 18 is a mistake here, because this is a single strand, not a double helix.
column29: How many sugars are in one nucleotide?

column9: A short DNA segment is 20 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain in all?
column28: Each base pair is made of two nucleotides, one from each strand, so 20 × 2 = 40. Answering 20 counts only one strand.
column29: A base pair has one nucleotide from each strand.

column9: The four nitrogen bases in DNA are adenine, thymine, guanine and ___.
column28: The fourth base is cytosine (C), which pairs with guanine. Uracil is a base, but it is found in RNA instead of thymine, not in DNA.
column29: This base pairs with guanine.

column9: A sample of salmon DNA is 26% adenine. What percent of its bases are cytosine?
column28: A = T, so T = 26% and A + T = 52%. That leaves 100 − 52 = 48% for C and G, split evenly: C = 24%. Answering 48 forgets to split the leftover between C and G.
column29: Find T first, then figure out what percent is left for C and G together.

column9: A sample of sea urchin DNA is 31% guanine. What percent of its bases are thymine?
column28: G = C, so C = 31% and C + G = 62%. That leaves 38% for A and T, split evenly: T = 19%. Answering 38 forgets to divide by 2, and answering 31 pairs T with G.
column29: G's partner has the same percent. Then subtract both from 100.

column9: A DNA sample from a mushroom is 12% adenine. What percent of its bases are guanine?
column28: A = T = 12%, so A + T = 24%. That leaves 76% for C and G, and half of it is G: 38%. Picking 76% forgets to split the leftover between C and G.
column29: Find A + T first, subtract from 100, then remember C and G share what is left.

column9: A DNA sample from a fruit fly is 27% cytosine. Which set of percentages for the other bases is correct?
column28: G = C = 27%, so C + G = 54%, which leaves 46% for A and T: 23% each. Choosing 46% for each forgets to split, and setting A equal to C pairs the wrong bases.
column29: Use the pairs: C matches G, and A matches T. All four must add to 100%.

column9: A lab measures the bases in a sample of human DNA: A = 30.9%, T = 29.4%, G = 19.9%, C = 19.8%. Which conclusion fits these data best?
column14: A and T are about equal, as are G and C, which supports A pairing with T and G with C
column15: A and G are about equal, so A must pair with G
column16: All four bases are found in equal amounts
column17: The sample must be RNA, because the numbers are not exactly equal and RNA is single-stranded
column28: A ≈ T and G ≈ C, which is Chargaff's rule and matches the A–T, C–G pairing in the double helix. Small differences come from measurement error. A (30.9%) and G (19.9%) are not close, and the bases are clearly not all equal.
column29: Compare the bases in pairs. Which two numbers are close to each other?

column9: Which pair of strands is correctly matched by the base pairing rule?
column28: Pair each base: A–T, T–A, C–G, G–C, G–C, A–T, so ATCGGA matches TAGCCT. The first choice has the last pair wrong (A–A), the second uses U (an RNA base), and the last copies the strand instead of pairing it.
column29: Check every position, all the way to the last letter.

column9: A section of a fruit fly gene reads TTGACCGA on one strand. The complementary strand reads ___.
column20: AACTGGCT|A A C T G G C T|A-A-C-T-G-G-C-T|A, A, C, T, G, G, C, T|A,A,C,T,G,G,C,T
column28: T→A, T→A, G→C, A→T, C→G, C→G, G→C, A→T gives AACTGGCT. Losing your place in a long strand is the most common error, so pair one base at a time and count that you have 8 letters.
column29: Work left to right and check that your answer has the same number of letters.

column9: In a DNA diagram, one strand reads T G C A and the strand directly across from it reads A _ G T. The missing base is ___ (type one letter).
column28: The missing base is across from G, and G pairs with C. Writing G (copying the top strand) is the common mistake.
column29: Line up the strands. Which base is directly across from the blank?

column9: Select every statement that correctly describes the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA. Select all that apply.
column14: It forms the sides of the DNA ladder
column15: Sugars and phosphates alternate along it
column16: It runs the whole length of each strand
column17: It is made of nitrogen bases
column18: It holds the two strands together across the middle
column28: The backbone is the long side of each strand: sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate along its whole length. The bases (not the backbone) pair across the middle to hold the strands together, and uracil is only in RNA.
column29: The backbone is made of two of the three parts of a nucleotide. Which part is left out?

column9: Select every way that the structure of DNA is different from the structure of RNA. Select all that apply.
column14: DNA has the sugar deoxyribose, while RNA has ribose
column15: DNA has thymine, while RNA has uracil in its place
column16: DNA is usually double-stranded, while RNA is usually single-stranded
column18: DNA is made of amino acids
column19: DNA has uracil, while RNA has thymine
column28: DNA differs from RNA in its sugar (deoxyribose vs ribose), one base (thymine vs uracil) and number of strands (two vs one). Both have phosphate groups, neither is made of amino acids, and the last choice has thymine and uracil backward.
column29: Compare the three parts of a nucleotide, then count the strands.

column9: A DNA sample is 20% adenine. Select every statement that is true. Select all that apply.
column28: T = A = 20%, so A + T = 40%. The other 60% is split evenly: G = 30% and C = 30%. Saying C = 60% forgets to split, and G = 20% pairs G with A.
column29: Find T and A + T first, then share what is left between C and G.

column9: Watson and Crick drew on several sources of information and methods to build their double helix model. Select every one they actually used. Select all that apply.
column14: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images of DNA
column15: Chargaff's data showing A = T and C = G
column16: Building physical models out of metal and cardboard pieces
column17: Light microscope photos clearly showing the twisted strands
column18: A complete sequence of the human genome
column28: Watson and Crick combined Franklin's X-ray data, Chargaff's base ratios and hands-on model building. DNA is far too thin to see twisting with a light microscope, and the human genome and DNA fingerprinting came decades after 1953.
column29: Think about what existed in the early 1950s.

column9: Adenine and guanine are large bases with two rings. Thymine and cytosine are small bases with one ring. Why can't adenine pair with guanine in the double helix?
column14: Two large bases together would be too wide to fit between the two backbones
column15: Adenine and guanine are found on different chromosomes, so they never meet in the same helix
column17: There is no reason; the pairing is random
column28: Every rung is one large base plus one small base, so all rungs are the same width. A large plus large pair would be too wide. Guanine pairs with cytosine in DNA, and the pairing is not random.
column29: Picture a rung made of two big pieces. Would it fit in a ladder where every other rung is big + small?

column9: A student's paper model of DNA shows a rung made of cytosine paired with thymine. What is wrong with this rung?
column14: Nothing is wrong; any two bases can pair
column15: Cytosine pairs only with guanine, so this rung breaks the base pairing rule
column17: A rung should be made of sugar, not bases, since the bases belong on the outside of the ladder
column28: In DNA, C pairs only with G and T pairs only with A. A C–T rung breaks the rule, and two small bases would also make the rung too narrow. Uracil is not in DNA.
column29: Each base has exactly one partner. Who is cytosine's partner?

column9: Match each base to its description.
column14: Adenine :: A large two-ring base that pairs with thymine
column15: Guanine :: A large two-ring base that pairs with cytosine
column16: Thymine :: A small one-ring base, found only in DNA, that pairs with adenine
column17: Cytosine :: A small one-ring base that pairs with guanine
column18: Uracil :: A small base found in RNA in place of thymine
column28: A and G are the large two-ring bases; T and C are the small one-ring bases. Each pair is one large and one small base (A–T, G–C). Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.
column29: Sort the bases into large (A, G) and small (T, C) first, then use the pairs.

column9: Match each scientist to the contribution they made.
column14: Rosalind Franklin :: Made X-ray images of DNA, including Photo 51
column15: James Watson and Francis Crick :: Built the double helix model in 1953
column16: Erwin Chargaff :: Found that A = T and C = G in DNA samples
column17: Gregor Mendel :: Showed that traits are inherited in patterns, before DNA was understood
column28: Franklin provided the X-ray images, Chargaff the base ratios, and Watson and Crick put the evidence together in a model. Mendel's pea plant work came about 90 years earlier. Giving Watson and Crick credit for Photo 51 is a common mistake.
column29: Match the X-ray image and the base-ratio data first; the model came from combining them.

column9: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
column28: A nitrogen base is one part of a nucleotide; many nucleotides make a strand; two strands make the double helix; and a long double helix wrapped around proteins makes a chromosome. Putting nucleotide before base forgets that the base is inside the nucleotide.
column29: Each item is built from the one before it.

column9: Put these events in the order they happened, from earliest to latest.
column14: Watson and Crick publish the double helix model
column15: Mendel studies inheritance in pea plants
column17: Chargaff publishes that A = T and C = G
column28: Mendel's pea plant work was in the 1860s, Chargaff's base data around 1950, Photo 51 in 1952, and the Watson–Crick model in 1953. The model came last because it was built from the earlier evidence.
column29: The model was built using the other DNA evidence, so it must come after it.

column9: A segment of a tomato plant gene is 60 base pairs long. 25 of the pairs are A–T pairs. How many of the pairs are C–G pairs?
column28: Every base pair is either A–T (or T–A) or C–G (or G–C). 60 − 25 = 35 C–G pairs. Answering 25 assumes the two kinds must be equal, which is not true; only A = T and C = G.
column29: Every pair is one of two kinds.

column9: One full twist of the DNA double helix contains about 10 base pairs. About how many nucleotides are in a stretch of DNA that makes 7 full twists?
column28: 7 twists × 10 base pairs = 70 base pairs, and each base pair has 2 nucleotides: 70 × 2 = 140. Stopping at 70 counts base pairs, not nucleotides.
column29: First find the number of base pairs, then think about how many nucleotides are in each pair.

column9: Which of these base sequences could NOT be part of a DNA strand?
column28: TACUG contains U (uracil), which is found in RNA, not DNA. Any order of A, T, C and G can appear in a DNA strand, even long runs of one base like AAAAT.
column29: Look for a letter that does not belong in DNA.

column9: The two strands of a DNA double helix are described as antiparallel. What does antiparallel mean?
column14: The strands run in opposite directions, like two lanes of a highway
column15: The strands never touch each other
column16: The strands have identical base sequences, so they match each other letter for letter
column17: The strands are straight and never twist
column28: Antiparallel means the strands point in opposite directions: one runs up while its partner runs down. The strands do connect through base pairs, they are complementary rather than identical, and they twist into a helix.
column29: Anti- means opposite.

column9: A student says, 'If I know the base sequence of one strand of DNA, I also know the sequence of the other strand.' Is the student right?
column14: Yes, because the base pairing rule tells you each base's partner
column15: No, because the other strand's bases are random and can be in any order at all
column16: Yes, but only if the two strands are identical to each other in every base
column17: No, because the hydrogen bonds change the bases
column28: Because A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, one strand predicts the other exactly. The strands are complementary, not identical and not random. This is also why each strand can serve as a template.
column29: Does each base have one partner or many?

column9: Human DNA and banana DNA are made of the same four bases and have the same double helix shape. What makes human DNA different from banana DNA?
column14: Human DNA uses a different sugar
column17: Human bases are larger than banana bases
column28: All organisms use the same nucleotides and the same double helix. What differs is the sequence of bases, just as the same 26 letters can spell different books. The sugar, the number of strands and the size of the bases are the same.
column29: Think about how the same letters can spell different words.

column9: A DNA model kit has 12 phosphate pieces, 12 sugar pieces and 12 base pieces, with the right kinds of bases to pair. What is the longest double-stranded DNA model you can build?
column28: Each nucleotide needs one phosphate, one sugar and one base, so the kit makes 12 nucleotides. Each base pair needs 2 nucleotides, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6 base pairs. Answering 12 forgets that a base pair uses two nucleotides.
column29: First count how many full nucleotides you can make.

column9: Select every base pair that could appear as a rung in a DNA double helix. Select all that apply.
column28: A–T, T–A and G–C all follow the rule; the order you read the pair in does not matter. A–G and C–T break the rule, and A–U happens only in RNA.
column29: T–A is the same pair as A–T read from the other side.

column9: Which statement correctly compares the bonds in DNA?
column14: The backbone is held by strong covalent bonds, and the base pairs are held by weak hydrogen bonds
column15: Both the backbone and the base pairs are held by weak hydrogen bonds, so the strands come apart easily
column16: The backbone is held by weak bonds, and the base pairs by strong bonds
column17: Both are held by ionic bonds
column28: Strong covalent bonds link sugar to phosphate along each strand, so the base order stays fixed. Weak hydrogen bonds hold the pairs together, so the strands can be separated. Reversing these is a common mistake.
column29: Which part has to come apart easily when DNA unzips?

column9: A double-stranded gumdrop model of DNA uses 40 gumdrops for bases in all. 14 of them are green (cytosine). How many are red (adenine)?
column28: C = G, so there are 14 guanine and 28 C + G. That leaves 40 − 28 = 12 for A and T, split evenly: 6 adenine. Answering 12 forgets that A and T share the leftover.
column29: Count C and G together first, then split what is left.

column9: In a sample of wheat DNA, adenine and thymine together make up 58% of the bases. What percent of the bases are guanine?
column28: 100 − 58 = 42% is cytosine plus guanine, and C = G, so G = 21%. Answering 42 forgets to split between C and G, and answering 29 gives the percent of adenine instead.
column29: What percent is left for C and G together?

column9: A DNA diagram shows each nucleotide as three shapes: (1) a circle, (2) a pentagon and (3) a rectangle that touches a rectangle from the other strand. Which shape is the nitrogen base?
column17: None of them; bases are not shown in diagrams
column28: The base is the part that reaches across and pairs with a base on the other strand, so it is the rectangle. In most diagrams the circle is the phosphate and the pentagon is the five-carbon sugar. Picking the sugar is a common mistake because the base attaches to it.
column29: Which part of a nucleotide meets a partner from the other strand?

column9: A DNA molecule contains 1,000 bases in all. 300 of them are cytosine. How many are adenine?
column28: G = C = 300, so C + G = 600. That leaves 1,000 − 600 = 400 for A and T, split evenly: 200 adenine. Answering 400 forgets to split, and answering 700 subtracts only cytosine.
column29: Account for cytosine's partner before you subtract from the total.

column9: An A–T pair is held together by 2 hydrogen bonds, and a C–G pair is held together by 3. A short DNA segment has 6 A–T pairs and 4 C–G pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
column28: 6 A–T pairs × 2 = 12, and 4 C–G pairs × 3 = 12, so 12 + 12 = 24 hydrogen bonds. A common mistake is counting one bond per pair (10) or using 3 for every pair (30).
column29: Find the bonds for each kind of pair separately, then add.

column9: An A–T pair is held by 2 hydrogen bonds and a C–G pair by 3. Two DNA samples are heated until their strands separate. Sample X is 35% adenine. Sample Y is 15% adenine. Which sample needs a higher temperature to separate, and why?
column14: Sample Y, because it has more C–G pairs, which have more hydrogen bonds
column15: Sample X, because it has more A–T pairs, which have more hydrogen bonds
column16: Both samples separate at the same temperature, since all DNA has the same bonds
column17: Sample X, because adenine is the heaviest base
column28: Sample Y is 15% A, so A + T = 30% and C + G = 70%. Sample X has only 30% C + G. More C–G pairs means more hydrogen bonds to break, so Y needs more heat. Choosing X confuses which pair has 3 bonds.
column29: Use Chargaff's rule to find the percent of C + G in each sample.

column9: One strand of a DNA segment reads ATGCCGTATG. Counting BOTH strands, how many guanine (G) bases are in the segment?
column28: The given strand has 3 G's. The other strand has a G across from every C on the given strand, and there are 2 C's, so it has 2 G's. 3 + 2 = 5. Answering 3 forgets the second strand.
column29: Count the G's you can see, then count the C's: each C has a G across from it.

column9: A student reports these results for a sample of double-stranded DNA: A = 28%, T = 28%, G = 28%, C = 16%. What is wrong with these results?
column14: G and C should be equal, so these numbers cannot be right for double-stranded DNA
column15: A and G should be equal
column16: The four percentages should add up to 50%, not 100%
column17: Nothing is wrong; the numbers add up to 100%
column28: In double-stranded DNA every G is paired with a C, so G must equal C. Here G = 28% but C = 16%, which breaks Chargaff's rule. Adding up to 100% is necessary but not enough.
column29: Check each base against its partner.

column9: Scientists analyze the DNA of a small virus and find A = 25%, T = 33%, G = 24%, C = 18%. What is the best conclusion?
column14: Its DNA is probably single-stranded, because A does not equal T and G does not equal C
column15: Its DNA is a normal double helix
column17: The virus has too many bases to be DNA
column28: Chargaff's rule (A = T, C = G) holds only when bases are paired in two strands. Here neither pair matches, so the bases are not paired: the DNA is most likely single-stranded. Some viruses really do have single-stranded DNA.
column29: Chargaff's rule works because of base pairing. What if there is nothing to pair with?

column9: A classmate builds a DNA model with the nitrogen bases on the outside and the sugar-phosphate backbones in the center. Which evidence best shows that the bases must be on the inside instead?
column14: DNA is found in the nucleus of most cells
column15: Chargaff's finding that A = T and C = G, which suggests bases pair with each other across the middle
column16: DNA has four kinds of bases
column28: A = T and C = G suggests that each A is matched with a T and each C with a G, which only works if the bases face each other in the middle of the helix. The other facts are true but say nothing about where the bases sit.
column29: Which evidence tells you the bases have partners?

column9: Select every connection in DNA that is a strong covalent bond rather than a hydrogen bond. Select all that apply.
column14: Sugar to phosphate along one strand
column15: Sugar to the nitrogen base within one nucleotide
column16: Adenine to thymine across the helix
column17: Cytosine to guanine across the helix
column18: Atoms within the deoxyribose sugar ring
column28: All the bonds inside a strand are covalent: sugar to phosphate, sugar to base and the atoms within the sugar. Only the connections between paired bases across the helix (A to T, C to G) are hydrogen bonds. Calling every DNA bond a hydrogen bond is the common mistake.
column29: Hydrogen bonds connect the two strands. Everything within one strand is held more strongly.

column9: Select every reason the double helix structure is good for storing and copying genetic information. Select all that apply.
column14: The bases can be in any order along a strand, so they can carry many different messages
column15: Complementary pairing means each strand can serve as a template for the other
column16: Weak hydrogen bonds let the strands separate without breaking the backbone
column17: Strong bonds in the backbone keep the order of the bases from falling apart
column18: The bases change partners randomly, which creates variety
column19: DNA is single-stranded, so it is easy to read
column28: Sequence carries the message, complementary pairing allows copying, weak hydrogen bonds allow unzipping, and the strong backbone protects the order. Bases do not swap partners randomly, and DNA is double-stranded, not single-stranded.
column29: Check each choice against what you know about bonds and pairing.

column9: A section of a bean plant gene reads CGTTAGCCAT on one strand. The complementary strand reads ___.
column20: GCAATCGGTA|G C A A T C G G T A|G-C-A-A-T-C-G-G-T-A|G, C, A, A, T, C, G, G, T, A|G,C,A,A,T,C,G,G,T,A
column28: C→G, G→C, T→A, T→A, A→T, G→C, C→G, C→G, A→T, T→A gives GCAATCGGTA. In long strands the common errors are skipping a letter or slipping into A–G pairing, so check that your answer has 10 letters.
column29: Work in small chunks of 2 or 3 letters and check the length at the end.

column9: A bacterial DNA molecule has 4,000 nucleotides, and 24% of them are thymine. How many guanine nucleotides does it have?
column28: A = T = 24%, so A + T = 48%. That leaves 52% for C and G, so G = 26%. 26% of 4,000 = 0.26 × 4,000 = 1,040. A common mistake is stopping at the percent (26) or using 52% instead of 26%.
column29: Find the percent of guanine first, then take that percent of 4,000.

column9: A double-stranded DNA segment contains 120 guanine bases and 80 thymine bases. How many nucleotides are in the whole segment?
column28: C = G = 120 and A = T = 80, so the total is 120 + 120 + 80 + 80 = 400. Answering 200 adds only the two given bases and forgets their partners.
column29: Each given base has a partner present in the same amount.

column9: An A–T pair has 2 hydrogen bonds and a C–G pair has 3. A DNA segment is 50 base pairs long and is held together by 130 hydrogen bonds in all. How many of its base pairs are C–G pairs?
column28: If all 50 pairs were A–T there would be 100 hydrogen bonds. Each C–G pair adds 1 more bond, and there are 130 − 100 = 30 extra bonds, so there are 30 C–G pairs (and 20 A–T pairs). Check: 30 × 3 + 20 × 2 = 90 + 40 = 130.
column29: Start by imagining all 50 pairs are A–T. How many extra bonds are there?

column9: A double-stranded DNA segment has 300 nucleotides, and 90 of them are cytosine. What percent of the nucleotides are adenine?
column28: 90 ÷ 300 = 30% cytosine, so G = 30% and C + G = 60%. That leaves 40% for A and T: A = 20%. Answering 70 subtracts only cytosine, and answering 40 forgets to split between A and T.
column29: Turn the cytosine count into a percent first.

column9: Within ONE strand of a DNA molecule, 20% of the bases are adenine and 30% are thymine. What percent of the bases on the OTHER strand are adenine?
column28: Every T on the first strand has an A across from it on the other strand, so the other strand's adenine equals the first strand's thymine: 30%. Chargaff's A = T rule applies to the whole double helix, not within a single strand, which is the trap behind 20%.
column29: The A's on the second strand sit across from which base on the first strand?

column9: Within ONE strand of a DNA molecule, 10% of the bases are adenine and 40% are thymine. What percent of the bases in the WHOLE double-stranded molecule are adenine?
column28: Strand 1 has 10% A. Strand 2 has an A across from every T on strand 1, so it is 40% A. Both strands are the same length, so the whole molecule is (10 + 40) ÷ 2 = 25% A. Answering 10 uses only one strand; answering 50 adds without averaging.
column29: Find the percent of A on each strand, then average them.

column9: Imagine walking straight across one rung of the DNA ladder, from one side to the other. Put the parts in the order you would cross them.
column28: Start at the backbone of strand 1, cross its base, the hydrogen bonds in the middle, the partner base on strand 2, and end at the backbone of strand 2. The hydrogen bonds are in the very center, between the two bases.
column29: The structure is symmetrical: what is in the exact middle of a rung?

column9: You know the percent of guanine in a DNA sample and want the percent of adenine. Put the steps in order.
column15: Divide what is left by 2 to get the percent of adenine
column16: Write that cytosine has the same percent as guanine
column17: Add the percents of cytosine and guanine
column28: First use C = G, then add C + G, subtract from 100% to find A + T, and finally divide by 2 because A = T. Forgetting the last step (dividing by 2) is the most common error.
column29: You cannot subtract from 100% until you know how much C and G take up together.

column9: Chargaff found that A = T and C = G in DNA, but that A does not usually equal C. How did this help Watson and Crick?
column14: It suggested that A pairs with T and C pairs with G across the two strands
column15: It showed that DNA is a single strand
column16: It proved that DNA is shaped like a helix
column17: It showed that the backbone is made of sugar and phosphate
column28: Equal amounts of A and T (and of C and G) in every sample hinted that these bases are partners. The helix shape came from Franklin's X-ray images, not Chargaff's data, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Why would two bases always be found in exactly equal amounts?

column9: Suppose a damaged spot in DNA caused two large two-ring bases to pair with each other at one rung. What would most likely happen to the double helix at that spot?
column14: Nothing, because all rungs are flexible
column15: The rung would be too wide, making a bulge in the otherwise even helix
column16: That section would turn into RNA
column17: The backbone there would become hydrogen bonds
column28: Normal rungs are one large plus one small base, so the helix has a constant width. Two large bases make a rung that is too wide and distorts the helix. Cells have repair enzymes that can detect this kind of distortion.
column29: Think about why every normal rung is the same width.

column9: A forensic lab finds that a DNA sample from a hair root is 34% cytosine. Select every result the lab should also expect. Select all that apply.
column28: C = G = 34%, so C + G = 68%. A + T = 100 − 68 = 32%, so A = T = 16%. Setting A equal to C is the pairing mistake, and 33% or 66% come from subtracting before doubling.
column29: Double the cytosine percent first, then subtract from 100.

column9: Each DNA strand has a 5′ end and a 3′ end, and the two strands are antiparallel. One strand reads 5′-ATGC-3′. Which choice correctly shows its partner strand lined up underneath it?
column28: The partner bases are TACG (A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G), and because the strands are antiparallel the partner runs the opposite way, 3′ to 5′. 5′-TACG-3′ has the right bases pointing the wrong way, UACG uses an RNA base, and ATGC copies the strand.
column29: Get the bases right first, then flip the direction labels.

column9: A short stretch of DNA contains only A and T bases, with no C or G at all. Could this stretch still form a normal double helix?
column14: Yes; as long as each A pairs with a T, every rung follows the base pairing rule
column15: No; every DNA molecule must contain all four bases in equal amounts to make a double helix
column16: No; without G there is nothing to build the backbone from
column17: Yes, but it would have to be RNA
column28: Base pairing only requires that each A sits across from a T and each C across from a G. A stretch of only A–T pairs follows the rule (and A = T still holds). Chargaff's rule does not say all four bases are equal, and the backbone is sugar and phosphate, not bases.
column29: Chargaff's rule compares partners, not all four bases.

column9: Each nucleotide has one phosphate group, one sugar and one nitrogen base. A double-stranded DNA segment is 45 base pairs long. How many phosphate groups, sugars and bases does it have in all (add all three together)?
column28: 45 base pairs × 2 = 90 nucleotides, and each nucleotide has 3 parts, so 90 × 3 = 270. Answering 135 forgets that each base pair has two nucleotides.
column29: First find the number of nucleotides.

column9: Along ONE strand of DNA (not across the rungs), which rule controls the order of the bases?
column14: A must always be followed by T
column15: The bases must alternate large, small, large, small
column16: There is no pairing rule along a strand; any order is possible, and that order carries the information
column17: The sequence must repeat ATCG over and over
column28: The base pairing rule works across the two strands, not along one strand. Along a strand, bases can be in any order, and that variety is what lets DNA store different genes. Applying the pairing rule along a strand is a common misunderstanding.
column29: The pairing rule is about partners on opposite strands.
